Dolph Lundgren: Hans "Dolph" Lundgren (Swedish: [ˈdɔlːf ˈlɵ̌nːdɡreːn]; born 3 November 1957) is a Swedish-American actor, filmmaker, and martial artist.
In what year was Molybdenum discovered?
Molybdenum is a chemical element; it has symbol Mo and atomic number 42.
In what year was Titanium discovered?
Titanium is a chemical element; it has symbol Ti and atomic number 22.
Mikoyan MiG-27: Russian Aircraft Corporation MiG. It is based on the Mikoyan-Gurevich MiG-23 fighter aircraft, but optimised for air-to-ground attack.
Which country is Northrop Grumman B-21 Raider from?

Northrop Grumman B-21 Raider: United States. Part of the Long Range Strike Bomber (LRS-B) program, it is to be an intercontinental strategic bomber that can deliver conventional and thermonuclear weapons.
Who is credited with discovering Indium?
Indium: Ferdinand Reich. Indium is a chemical element; its symbol is In and its atomic number is 49.
Who is credited with discovering Californium?
Californium: Stanley Gerald Thompson. Californium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Cf and atomic number 98.
Who is credited with discovering Fluorine?
Fluorine: Henri Moissan. Fluorine is a chemical element; it has symbol F and atomic number 9.
This is the most common genetic cause of dwarfism, typically producing short arms and legs with a normal-length torso and an enlarged head with a prominent forehead — what condition is it?
Achondroplasia is a genetic disorder whose primary feature is dwarfism.
Often caused by misaligned or unevenly focused eyes in early childhood, this is the most common cause of single-eye vision loss in kids and young adults, nicknamed 'lazy eye' — what condition is it?
Amblyopia is a disorder of sight in which the brain fails to fully process input from one eye and over time favors the other eye.
A physician who called medicine his lawful wife and literature his mistress, this Russian writer produced four stage classics and ranks among modernism's founders — who is he?
Anton Chekhov was Russian dramatist and author (1860–1904).
Which genus of early hominins, which lived in Africa during the Pliocene and Early Pleistocene, gave rise to the genera Homo, Paranthropus, and Kenyanthropus?
Australopithecus (-loh-; or, os-, from Latin australis southern 'grc' and (pthkos) ape) is a genus of early hominins that existed in Africa during the Pliocene and Early Pleistocene.
This red-orange compound, formed from the breakdown of heme, is further processed into pigments that give feces their brown color and urine its straw-yellow hue. What is it?
Bilirubin (BR) (adopted from German, originally bili, for bile, plus ruber, Latin for red) is a red-orange compound that occurs as the reduction product of biliverdin, a breakdown product of heme.

Named for its bread-like texture and potato-like flavor when cooked, this tropical tree fruit spread through Oceania via ancient seafaring migrations before European navigators brought Polynesian varieties to the Caribbean — which fruit?
Breadfruit (Artocarpus altilis) is a species of flowering tree in the mulberry and jackfruit family (Moraceae).
Discovered in 1940, this non-intoxicating compound extracted from cannabis is used medically as an anticonvulsant for two rare, severe forms of childhood epilepsy — what is it?
Cannabidiol (CBD) is a phytocannabinoid, one of 113 identified cannabinoids in Cannabis, along with tetrahydrocannabinol (THC), and accounts for up to 40% of the plant's extract.

The scientific study of matter's properties and behavior, this physical science occupies an intermediate position between physics and biology, sometimes called the central science. What is this field of study?
Chemistry is the scientific study of the properties and behavior of matter. Chemistry also addresses the nature of chemical bonds in chemical compounds.
Domed-backed little beetles that mostly hunt aphids, they wear aposematic spots to warn off predators and are named for 'lady' Mary — what's the scientific family?
Coccinellidae is a widespread family of small beetles.

Though Colin Maclaurin published special cases two years earlier, this determinant-based method for solving linear systems bears the name of the mathematician who generalized it in 1750 — what's it known as?
Cramer's rule is an explicit formula for the solution of a system of linear equations with as many equations as unknowns, valid whenever the system has a unique solution.

Distinguished from their one-leaved cousins by a pair of embryonic seed leaves, this classic angiosperm classification was shown by molecular science not to form a single evolutionary lineage — which plant group?
Dicotyledon (or, more rarely, dicotyls), are one of the two groups into which all the flowering plants (angiosperms) were formerly divided.
Born in North Carolina in 1983, this former NSA contractor leaked classified files exposing global surveillance programs after working for the CIA, Dell, and a defense contractor — name him?

Edward Snowden (born June 21, 1983) is a former United States National Security Agency (NSA) intelligence contractor who leaked classified documents revealing the existence of global surveillance programs.
Also called grain alcohol, this volatile compound with the formula C2H5OH is the active ingredient in every alcoholic beverage — what is it?
Ethanol (also called ethyl alcohol, grain alcohol, drinking alcohol, or simply alcohol) is an organic compound with the chemical formula CH3CH2OH.
This everyday bodily process — expelling gas from the intestines through the anus — has its own dedicated field of scientific study named after it: what's the term for the process itself?
Flatulence is the expulsion of gas from the intestines via the anus, commonly referred to as farting.
Ordained a priest in 1923, this Belgian physicist connected an expanding universe to Einstein's field equations and floated an early Big Bang hypothesis — who was he?
Georges Lemaître (lə-MET-rə; 17 July 1894 - 20 June 1966) was a Belgian Catholic priest, theoretical physicist, and mathematician who made major contributions to cosmology and astrophysics.
Born Herman Webster Mudgett, this con artist and killer worked his crimes around the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition, earning the nickname "the Beast of Chicago" — who was he?
H. H. Holmes (May 16, 1861 - May 7, 1896), better known as Dr.

Often called the "father of the Indian nuclear programme," this theoretical physicist founded the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research and the research centre later renamed in his honour. Who was he?
Homi J. Bhabha (30 October 1909 - 24 January 1966) was an Indian nuclear theoretical physicist who is widely credited as the "father of the Indian nuclear programme".

Dubbed the 'saviour of mothers,' this 19th-century Hungarian doctor demonstrated that a simple hygiene practice could drastically cut deaths from childbed fever, decades before germ theory was widely accepted — who is he?

Ignaz Semmelweis (1 July 1818 - 13 August 1865) was a Hungarian medical doctor and scientist of German descent who was an early pioneer of antiseptic procedures and was described as the "saviour of mothers".
Most of the flowers used by the global perfume industry for this fragrant genus of shrubs and vines are grown in a single Egyptian village. What plant is it?
Jasmine (botanical name: Jasminum) is a genus of shrubs and vines in the olive family of Oleaceae.
Diagnosed via corneal topography and linked to frequent eye rubbing and allergies, this progressive disorder causes the cornea to bulge into a cone shape — which eye condition?
Keratoconus is an eye disorder in which the cornea, the transparent front part of the eye, gradually thins and bulges outward into a cone shape.
Caused by Mycobacterium bacteria, this ancient nerve-damaging disease can dull a person's sense of pain so badly that unnoticed wounds cost them their fingers and toes — what is it?
Leprosy (HD), is a long-term infection by the bacterium Mycobacterium leprae or Mycobacterium lepromatosis.
Born in Vienna into one of Europe's richest families, this philosopher studied under Bertrand Russell at Cambridge and transformed 20th-century philosophy of language and logic — who is he?

Ludwig Wittgenstein ((h)tyne; Austrian; 26 April 1889 - 29 April 1951) was an Austro-British philosopher who worked in logic, philosophy of mathematics, philosophy of mind, and philosophy of language.

In 1835 she and Caroline Herschel became the first female Honorary Members of the Royal Astronomical Society, and decades later this Scottish polymath's name topped John Stuart Mill's women's-suffrage petition. Who is she?
Mary Somerville (ne Fairfax, formerly Greig; 1780-1872) was a Scottish scientist, writer, and polymath.
Entering Soviet service in 1983 alongside the larger Su-27, this 'Fulcrum' air-superiority fighter was later adapted into a multirole jet — which aircraft is it?
Mikoyan MiG-29 (NATO reporting name: Fulcrum) is a twin-engine fighter aircraft designed in the Soviet Union.
When the radial fibres of the iris over-dilate the pupil beyond its normal light response, what do doctors call this condition?
Mydriasis is the dilation of the pupil, usually having a non-physiological cause, or sometimes a physiological pupillary response.
Nicknamed the 'winter vomiting disease' and the most common cause of gastroenteritis, this fecal–orally spread bug usually strikes about 24 hours after exposure. What is it?
Norovirus is the most common cause of gastroenteritis. Norovirus, also known as Norwalk virus, is the most common cause of gastroenteritis.
Making up most of Earth's crust, this class of chemical compounds pairs oxygen with at least one other element — even the thin protective skin on aluminum foil counts as one — what's the class?
Oxide is a chemical compound containing at least one oxygen atom and one other element in its chemical formula.
Named from Greek words for 'odd' and 'toe,' this mammalian order groups horses, rhinoceroses, and tapirs together based on their toe count. Which order?
Perissodactyla (from Ancient Greek, perisss 'odd' and, dktylos 'finger, toe'), or odd-toed ungulates, is an order of ungulates.

This common skin condition begins with a single scaly 'herald patch,' followed weeks later by an eruption of smaller pinkish spots, and typically clears on its own within three months. What is it called?
Pityriasis rosea is a type of skin rash.
Roaming the interior of western and central North America, this even-toed mammal survived the Pleistocene extinction of its close relatives and evolved to resemble an antelope — which creature is it?
Pronghorn (Antilocapra americana) is a species of artiodactyl (even-toed, hoofed) mammal indigenous to interior western and central North America.

Distinguished from their smaller rodent cousins mainly by size, these long-tailed rodents span dozens of genera worldwide, with Rattus being the most familiar — of the 56 known species, what are they collectively called?
Rat are various medium-sized, long-tailed rodents.

Originally bred in Germany to herd livestock and pull carts of butchered meat to market until railways took over in the mid-1800s, this medium-to-large mastiff-type dog now also works as a guard and police dog - name the breed?
Rottweiler (UK also) is a breed of domestic mastiff type dog, regarded as medium-to-large or large.
Made by Novo Nordisk and taken by injection or pill, this peptide medicine doubles as a diabetes treatment and a weight-management drug — what is it?
Semaglutide is an anti-diabetic medication used for the treatment of type 2 diabetes, and an anti-obesity medication used for weight management.

With the formula NaNO3 and historically mined in massive deposits in Chile, this white, deliquescent salt is a key industrial source used to make fertilizers, pyrotechnics, and explosives — which compound?
Sodium nitrate is the chemical compound with the formula NaNO3. The mineral form is also known as nitratine, nitratite or soda niter.

Tracing its lineage back to ancestral fish from the Early Jurassic period roughly 174 to 201 million years ago, this family of 27 fish species is one of only two living branches of an ancient order that also includes the paddlefish — name this fish family?
Sturgeon are the 27 species of fish belonging to the family Acipenseridae.

Named for the order of fish that includes pufferfish, this potent neurotoxin also turns up in blue-ringed octopuses and rough-skinned newts, and is actually produced by symbiotic bacteria rather than the animals themselves — what's the toxin?

Tetrodotoxin (TTX) is a potent neurotoxin. Its name derives from Tetraodontiformes, an order that includes pufferfish, porcupinefish, ocean sunfish, and triggerfish; several of these species carry the toxin.
Not a single branch of the family of life but a strategy evolved over and over — a tall trunk and branches reaching for sunlight — describes which kind of perennial plant?
Tree is a perennial plant with an elongated stem, or trunk, usually supporting branches and leaves.

This flowering plant genus, the largest in its family with over 680 species, is found mostly across the temperate Northern Hemisphere but also as far-flung as Hawaii and the Andes. What is this plant commonly called?
Viola (plant) is a genus of flowering plants in the family Violaceae.
This mosquito-borne viral disease causes chills, nausea, and muscle pain, and in about 15% of cases progresses to liver damage that turns the skin a telltale color — what disease is it?
Yellow fever is a viral disease of typically short duration.
Caused by excess growth hormone after the body's growth plates have closed, this disorder first shows up as enlarged hands and feet before affecting the jaw and forehead — what condition is it?
Acromegaly: Human disease that results in excess growth of certain parts of the body.
Also called the Persian silk tree or mimosa tree, this flowering species in the pea family is native to Asia — what is it?

Albizia julibrissin: Species of plant. Albizia julibrissin, the Persian silk tree, pink silk tree, or mimosa tree, is a species of tree in the Fabaceae family, native to southwestern and eastern Asia.
This functional group, formed by replacing a carboxylic acid's hydroxyl with an amino group, creates the peptide bonds that link amino acids into proteins — what is it?
Amide: Organic compounds of the form RC(=O)NR′R″.

A German pharmacist coined this pigment's name from the Greek for 'flower' and 'dark blue' in 1835 — it shifts red to purple to blue depending on pH and colors blueberries, black rice, and autumn leaves; what is it?
A notoriously toxic metalloid and pnictogen with atomic number 33, it's used in lead alloys for car batteries and ammunition and as a semiconductor dopant — which element is it?
Arsenic: Chemical element with atomic number 33 (As). It is a metalloid and one of the pnictogens, and therefore shares many properties with its group 15 neighbors phosphorus and antimony.
This slender projection of a nerve cell typically carries electrical impulses away from the cell body toward other neurons, muscles, or glands — what is it called?
Axon: Long projection on a neuron that conducts signals to other neurons.
Named after the aromatic resin from which it was first derived, this simplest aromatic carboxylic compound forms salts widely used as food preservatives — what is it called?
This crested songbird in the crow family sports a black, U-shaped collar and is known for hiding acorns to eat later — which eastern North American bird?
Blue jay: Species of bird. The blue jay (Cyanocitta cristata) is a passerine bird in the family Corvidae, native to eastern North America.
This rhythmic process of inhaling and exhaling delivers oxygen to the alveoli and removes carbon dioxide, with its per-minute rate counted as a vital sign — what is it?
Breathing: Process of moving air in and out of the lungs.
With the formula CaC2, this industrial compound reacts with trace moisture to give off a garlicky smell and is used to generate acetylene gas in old-fashioned lamps — what is it?
Calcium carbide: Chemical compound. Its main use industrially is in the production of acetylene and calcium cyanamide.
This mammalian order of flesh-eating species is split into cat-like and dog-like suborders, Feliformia and Caniformia, and ranks as the sixth-largest order of mammals — which order?
Carnivora: Order of mammals. Carnivora ( kar-NIV-ər-ə) is an order of placental mammals specialised primarily in eating flesh, whose members are formally referred to as carnivorans.
Known in North America as fireweed and in Britain as rosebay willowherb, this perennial flowering plant thrives across the boreal forests of the Northern Hemisphere — which plant?
Chamaenerion angustifolium: Species of flowering plant in the willowherb family.

Native to Sri Lanka, the inner bark of this evergreen tree is the original source of a beloved baking spice, sometimes distinguished from a cheaper cousin as the 'true' or 'Ceylon' variety — which tree?
Cinnamomum verum: Species of tree. The inner bark of the tree is historically regarded as the spice cinnamon, though this term was later generalized to include C. cassia as well.
Making up a quarter to a third of all protein in mammals, this triple-helix fibrous protein needs vitamin C for its synthesis and gives structure to cartilage, tendons, and skin — what is it?
Collagen: Most abundant structural protein in animals.
First appearing in English in 1656 and later formalized in Latin by philosopher Christian Wolff, this field of study addresses the nature and origin of the universe — what field is it?
Cosmology: Study of the universe. Cosmology (from Ancient Greek κόσμος (cosmos) 'the universe, the world' and -λογία (logia) 'study of') is the study of the nature of the universe, the cosmos.
This biological process lets a cell make an exact copy of its genetic material by using each strand of the double helix as a template for a new one — what is it called?
DNA replication: Biological process. DNA replication ensures that each of the newly divided daughter cells receives its own copy of each DNA molecule.
A volatile, colorless liquid with a sweet, chloroform-like smell, this organochlorine (formula CH2Cl2) is slightly polar, won't mix with water, and is prized as a widely-used solvent. What is it?
Marketed as Cymbalta, this serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor treats depression, anxiety, and fibromyalgia pain — what is it?
This genus of deciduous trees, once popular as ornamental street trees across Europe and North America, was decimated by a fungal disease spread by bark beetles — which tree?
Elm: Flowering, deciduous trees, family Ulmaceae.

Defined by a single oxygen atom bridging two organyl groups (R−O−R′), this class of organic compounds includes a once-standard surgical anesthetic that lends its common one-word name to the whole family. What class of compound is this?
Ether: Organic compounds made of alkyl/aryl groups bound to oxygen (R–O–R')
Nicknamed the "Warthog" and flying since 1977, this straight-winged, twin-turbofan attack jet is the only U.S. production aircraft built solely for close air support against tanks — what is it?

Fairchild Republic A-10 Thunderbolt II: American close air support attack aircraft. In service since 1977, it is named after the Republic P-47 Thunderbolt strike-fighter of World War II, but is commonly referred to as the "Warthog".
Members of the order Siphonaptera, these flightless blood-sucking parasites can leap 50 times their own body length — what are they?
Flea: Insects of the order Siphonaptera. Flea, the common name for the order Siphonaptera, includes 2,500 species of small flightless insects that live as external parasites of mammals and birds.

Nicknamed for their nighttime cries, these small nocturnal African primates are, according to the African Wildlife Foundation, the continent's most successful strepsirrhine group — what are they commonly called?
Galago: Family of primates. The Ghanaian name aposor is given to them because of their firm grip on branches.
Found in the Eastern Atlantic and the Mediterranean, this prized food fish from the porgy family is a cornerstone of European aquaculture — which fish?
Gilt-head bream: Mediterranean fish. It is a highly esteemed food fish and an important species in aquaculture.
An Augustinian friar and abbot in Brno, this Austrian biologist spent 1856 to 1863 crossbreeding pea plants — work that earned him posthumous fame as the founder of genetics. Who was he?
Gregor Mendel: Austrian biologist and friar (1822–1884)

Made by fusing heavy nuclei in tiny quantities, this superheavy element 108 has a special isotope whose "magic numbers" of protons and neutrons make its deformed nucleus unusually stable — what is it?
Hassium: Chemical element with atomic number 108 (Hs)
Its name means 'river horse' in Ancient Greek, yet this semiaquatic sub-Saharan giant — the largest even-toed ungulate alive — is more closely tied to pigs than to horses; what is it?
Hippopotamus: Species of large semi-aquatic mammal.
Marketed as Buscopan, this anticholinergic medication treats abdominal cramps, bladder and biliary spasms, and can ease respiratory secretions near the end of life — what drug is it?
Hyoscine butylbromide: Anticholinergic medication. It is also used to improve excessive respiratory secretions at the end of life.
An application of computer science, this field covers not just computers and networks but also distribution technologies like television and telephones — what is it?
Information technology: Computer-based technologies. Whisler commented that "the new technology does not yet have a single established name.
Working under Tamerlane around 1400, this Persian astronomer and mathematician produced work that mostly never reached Europe and stays largely unpublished — who is it?
Jamshid al-Kashi: Persian astronomer and mathematician (c. 1380–1429)
Fluent in Quechua after being raised in two Indigenous households as a child, this Peruvian novelist and anthropologist became known for his intimate portrayals of Andean culture — who is he?
Caused by a thiamine deficiency often linked to heavy alcohol use, this brain disorder is marked by amnesia and confabulation, and frequently pairs with Wernicke encephalopathy — which condition?
Korsakoff syndrome: Mental illness caused by a lack of thiamine in the brain.
This Turing Award winner brought order to the chaos of distributed computing — and, on the side, created the document-preparation system LaTeX and wrote its first manual. Who is he?
Leslie Lamport: American computer scientist and mathematician (born 1941)
Genus name meaning 'horned' in Latin, this raptor nests in dense woodland edges but hunts over open ground, feeding mostly on voles — which bird?
Long-eared owl: Species of owl. The genus name, Asio, is Latin for "horned owl", and the specific epithet, otus, is derived from Greek and refers to a small eared owl.
A former mayor of Tehran and engineer by training, he served as Iran's sixth president from 2005 to 2013 and championed the country's nuclear program — who is he?

Mahmoud Ahmadinejad: President of Iran from 2005 to 2013. Mahmoud Ahmadinejad (né Sabbaghian; born 28 October 1956) is an Iranian politician who served as the sixth president of Iran from 2005 to 2013.

Belonging to the ancient order Ephemeroptera and keeping primitive traits like long tails and wings that won't fold flat, which aquatic insect's water-dwelling nymphs signal a clean, unpolluted stream?
Mayfly: Aquatic insects of the order Ephemeroptera. Over 3,000 species of mayfly are known worldwide, grouped into over 400 genera in 42 families.
This colorless gas, made by swapping one hydrogen atom in ammonia for a methyl group, has a strong rotten-fish smell and serves as a building block for many compounds — what is it?
Famous for mimicking the songs of other birds — and even singing well past midnight — this bird can recognize individual humans and is the state bird of five U.S. states. What kind of bird is it?
Mockingbird: Family of birds. The only mockingbird commonly found in North America is the northern mockingbird.

Named for being quieter than its relatives, this large white waterfowl carries an orange beak topped with a black knob that's bigger in males, and is more common in North America than in its native Europe — which bird?
Mute swan: Large species of waterfowl. The mute swan (Cygnus olor) is a species of swan and a member of the family Anatidae within the waterfowl order.
Described by Eric Kandel as the 'epic challenge' of biology, this multidisciplinary field studies the brain, spinal cord, and peripheral nervous system — what field is it?
Neuroscience: Scientific study of the nervous system.
Named for a discredited belief that it 'rows' itself with its pelvic fins, this family of long pelagic fish includes the longest bony fish alive at up to 8 meters?
Oarfish: Pelagic lampriform fish belonging to Regalecidae.
Derived from an ancient Roman unit called the uncia, this measure comes in an avoirdupois version equal to 1/16 of a pound and a heavier troy version used for precious metals — what unit is it?
Ounce: Unit of mass. The ounce is any of several different units of mass, weight, or volume and is derived almost unchanged from the uncia, an Ancient Roman unit of measurement.
He earned a PhD in physics from Cambridge for the first-ever thesis on quantum mechanics, then shared the 1933 Nobel Prize in Physics with Erwin Schrödinger — who is he?
Turning colorless in acid and a fuchsia pink in base, this phthalein dye is a favorite indicator for acid-base titrations — what is it?
Phenolphthalein: pH indicator that turns pink in basic solution.
Widely planted along London's streets as a hybrid variety, this tree genus includes the sycamores of North America and can tower up to 50 meters — which genus?
Platanus: Genus of flowering plants constituting the family Platanaceae.

Arising over 60 million years ago from small tree-dwellers, this order favored big brains, binocular color vision and opposable thumbs to grasp among the branches — and it includes lemurs and apes — what is it?
Primate: Order of mammals. New primate species continue to be discovered: over 25 species were described in the 2000s, 36 in the 2010s, and six in the 2020s.
Usually caused by E. coli spreading up the urinary tract, this kidney infection typically brings fever and flank tenderness, and can be prevented by urinating after sex — what condition is it?
Pyelonephritis: Inflammation of the kidney. It is typically due to a bacterial infection, most commonly Escherichia coli.
From a startled jump to a cat automatically reorienting itself mid-fall, this involuntary, split-second reaction runs through the nervous system without needing conscious thought — what's it called?
Reflex: Automatic, involuntary response to a stimulus.
Usually hidden underground, this plant organ anchors it in place while drawing in water and nutrients — what is it?
Root: Basal organ of a vascular plant.

With ears set low to detect prey moving underground and furry paw soles that insulate against scorching ground, this small desert feline was first described in the Algerian Sahara in 1858 — which animal?
Sand cat: Small wild cat species (Felis margarita)

Nicknamed the 'last Soviet citizen' for being aboard Mir when the USSR dissolved, this cosmonaut flew six missions and helped connect the first Russian and American modules of a space station — who is he?
Sergei Krikalev: Soviet and Russian cosmonaut (born 1958)
This big cat of the genus Panthera prowls the alpine zones of Central and South Asia at elevations of 3,000 to 4,500 meters, from the Himalayas to southern Siberia — what is it?
Snow leopard: Species of large felid.

Named after the patron saint of sailors, this luminous blue or violet glow appears around masts, spires, or aircraft during a strong electric field and can warn of an imminent lightning strike — what is this phenomenon called?
St. Elmo's fire: Luminous plasma created in an electric field.
Designed by R. J. Mitchell with a distinctive elliptical wing and sunken rivets for minimal drag, this was the only British fighter kept in continuous production throughout World War II — what is it?
Supermarine Spitfire: British single-seat WWII fighter aircraft.
Known as the barn funnel weaver in North America and simply the house spider in Europe, this species belongs to the funnel-web family Agelenidae — which arachnid?
Shaped like a butterfly and sitting in the neck just below the Adam's apple, this endocrine gland secretes hormones that regulate metabolic rate — which gland is it?
Thyroid: Endocrine gland in the neck. The lower two thirds of the lobes are connected by a thin band of tissue called the isthmus (pl.: isthmi).
This ester of glycerol and three fatty acids is the main constituent of body fat and a major component of human skin oils — what is it?
Triglyceride: Any ester of glycerol having all three hydroxyl groups esterified with fatty acids.

With co-researcher James Cronin, this American nuclear physicist won the 1980 Nobel for a 1964 K-meson experiment proving certain subatomic reactions aren't indifferent to time — discovering CP violation. Who was he?
Val Logsdon Fitch: American nuclear physicist. Born on a cattle ranch near Merriman, Nebraska, Fitch was drafted into the U.S.
Botanically a berry called a 'pepo,' this trailing vine's fruit comes in over 1,000 varieties and has a rind that's actually edible once cooked — what is it?
Spread mainly by the Aedes aegypti mosquito, this viral illness can cause a brief recovery before a relapse brings liver damage and jaundice — what disease is it?
Yellow fever: Viral disease. In most cases, symptoms include fever, chills, loss of appetite, nausea, muscle pains—particularly in the back—and headaches.
Gadolinium is denoted by which symbol?
The symbol for gadolinium is Gd. Gadolinium is a chemical element; it has symbol Gd and atomic number 64.
The symbol for chromium is Cr. Chromium is a chemical element; it has symbol Cr and atomic number 24.

In what year was Kirk Douglas born?
Kirk Douglas (born Issur Danielovitch; December 9, 1916 – February 5, 2020) was an American actor and filmmaker.
In what year was Kirstie Alley born?
Kirstie Alley: Kirstie Louise Alley (January 12, 1951 – December 5, 2022) was an American actress.
In what year was Samuel L. Jackson born?
Samuel L. Jackson: Samuel Leroy Jackson (born December 21, 1948) is an American actor and film producer.
In what year was Guy Ritchie born?
Guy Ritchie: Guy Stuart Ritchie (born 10 September 1968) is an English filmmaker known primarily for British comedy gangster films and large-scale action-adventure films.
In what year was Florence Pugh born?
Florence Pugh ( PEW; born 3 January 1996) is an English actress.
In what year was Bryan Cranston born?
Bryan Cranston: Bryan Lee Cranston (born March 7, 1956) is an American actor and filmmaker.
In what year was Mads Mikkelsen born?
Mads Mikkelsen: Mads Dittmann Mikkelsen (Danish: [ˈmæs ditsʰmɛːn ˈme̝kl̩sn̩]; born 22 November 1965) is a Danish actor.
In what year was Treat Williams born?
Treat Williams: Richard Treat Williams Jr. (December 1, 1951 – June 12, 2023) was an American actor, whose career on stage and in film and television spanned five decades.
